title: You Keep Asking Why God Hasn’t Sent Someone. Singleness Is Not Proof He Forgot Your Address.
paragraphs: You Keep Asking Why God Hasn’t Sent Someone. Singleness Is Not Proof He Forgot Your Address.
Maybe the hardest part of being single isn't sleeping alone. Maybe it's watching everyone else receive what you've been asking God for—and wondering why heaven seems to keep passing your address.
There is a particular kind of silence that happens after midnight.
The wedding photos have stopped scrolling.
The congratulations have stopped appearing.
The phone is face-down beside you.
And suddenly there is nobody left in the room except you, God, and the question you have tried very hard not to ask again.
“Lord… what about me?”
You love Him.
At least you're trying to.
You've prayed.
You've waited.
You've watched people who seemed less serious about God meet someone, fall in love, get engaged, get married, have children.
Meanwhile, you keep hearing the same Christian sentences.
“Your person is coming.”
“God is preparing somebody for you.”
“When you stop looking, that's when God will send them.”
“Just enjoy your season.”
“You'll understand when you meet the one.”
Sometimes those words are spoken by kind people who genuinely want to encourage you.
But when another birthday comes...
another wedding invitation arrives...
another relationship ends before it really begins...
another person asks why you're “still single”...
those sentences can start sounding less like encouragement and more like promises God Himself never actually made.
So perhaps somebody needs to tell you something more difficult.
And more compassionate.
And more biblical.
Your desire for marriage is not shameful.
Your loneliness is not imaginary.
Wanting somebody to come home to does not make you spiritually immature.
And singleness is not proof that God forgot your address.
But Scripture also does not promise every Christian a spouse.
That may sting.
Stay with me.
Because what sounds painful at first may actually rescue you from spending years measuring God's love by something He never promised.
Paul writes something remarkable in 1 Corinthians 7:32:
“Θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀμερίμνους εἶναι.”
Thelō de hymas amerimnous einai.
In context, the sense is: “I want you to be free from concern.”
Then Paul speaks directly about the unmarried believer:
“ὁ ἄγαμος μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κυρίου”
ho agamos merimna ta tou kyriou
“The unmarried person is concerned about the things of the Lord.”
And then comes Paul's destination:
“εὐπάρεδρον τῷ κυρίῳ ἀπερισπάστως”
The language points toward faithful, undistracted devotion to the Lord.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not look at unmarried Christians and say, “Don't worry. God is preparing your spouse.”
He does not call them incomplete Christians.
He does not describe them as people stuck in God's waiting room until their “real life” begins.
He gives singleness dignity.
He looks at a life without a spouse and sees something our relationship-obsessed culture often cannot imagine:
a life that can belong profoundly, fruitfully, beautifully to Christ.
And before somebody misunderstands Paul, he is not attacking marriage.
The same chapter makes clear that marrying is not sin. Marriage has God-given goodness, responsibilities, intimacy, sacrifice, and beauty.
Paul's point is not that marriage is dirty and singleness is holy.
His point is that marriage changes the distribution of your legitimate responsibilities.
The married believer has a spouse to love.
A household to consider.
Promises to keep.
Another human being whose needs cannot simply be ignored because ministry called.
Paul describes this reality with the Greek word μεμέρισται—memeristai—“is divided.”
Not divided between God and evil.
Divided among legitimate responsibilities.
That matters.
Because Paul is not describing singleness as an empty space where marriage should have been.
He sees it as a condition in which attention can be offered to Christ in ways that married believers may not have available to them.
And maybe that changes the question.
Maybe instead of only asking...
“God, when will You send somebody?”
there is another question worth trembling over:
“Jesus, what can I give You while my life is still arranged like this?”
That does not mean you have to stop wanting marriage.
You can want marriage deeply and still worship Jesus faithfully.
You can pray for a husband.
You can pray for a wife.
You can hope.
You can date wisely.
You can feel the ache of an empty passenger seat.
You can wish someone were sitting across from you at dinner.
You can cry when another relationship falls apart.
You can admit that sometimes the loneliness hurts so badly you don't want another sermon about “using your singleness.”
God does not require you to pretend pain isn't painful before He will call you faithful.
Jesus Himself knew loneliness.
He knew misunderstanding.
He knew rejection.
He knew what it meant to be surrounded by people and still carry something nobody around Him fully understood.
And most importantly for this conversation...
Jesus never married.
Think about what that means.
If marriage were necessary for a fully meaningful human life, then Christians would be forced into an impossible conclusion about the most complete human life ever lived.
Christ was not incomplete.
Christ was not waiting for romance to validate His existence.
Christ was not less human because He had no wife.
His identity was rooted in the Father.
His mission was obedience.
His love was poured out sacrificially.
His life was full.
And if you belong to Him, your deepest identity cannot finally be “single.”
It cannot finally be “married,” either.
It is in Christ.
Before somebody calls you husband...
before somebody calls you wife...
before somebody chooses you at an altar...
there was a Savior who chose to set His love upon sinners at immeasurable cost.
The Gospel is not the story of God finally sending you your soulmate.
The Gospel is the story of God sending His Son.
Jesus entered our brokenness.
He carried our sin.
He went willingly toward the cross.
He died for sinners.
He rose from the grave.
And He calls men and women everywhere to repent, believe, follow Him, and receive a life that no relationship status can manufacture.
That is where the deepest scandal becomes grace.
We were not merely lonely.
We were separated from God by sin.
And Christ came for us.
Maybe you've been asking God to send somebody because, underneath the request, another belief has quietly taken root:
“If somebody finally chooses me, I'll know I'm worth choosing.”
That is too much weight to put on another human being.
No husband can carry it.
No wife can carry it.
Marriage cannot be your resurrection.
Romance cannot be your gospel.
Another person's affection cannot cleanse your conscience, reconcile you to God, conquer death, or tell you who you ultimately are.
Only Jesus can occupy that throne without destroying you.
And this is where singleness can expose things we would rather leave hidden.
Sometimes we don't merely desire marriage.
Sometimes we have begun worshiping the future we imagine marriage will give us.
We picture the photos.
The house.
The children.
The anniversary.
The person reaching for our hand in church.
And without realizing it, we begin bargaining with God.
“I've stayed pure.”
“I've served You.”
“I've waited.”
“I didn't settle.”
“So where is my reward?”
But Jesus is not a vending machine into which we insert obedience until a spouse falls out.
Obedience is not currency used to purchase your preferred future.
We obey because He is Lord.
We love because He first loved us.
And grace means God owes us nothing...
yet in Christ He has given us what we could never deserve.
This is why unwanted singleness can become spiritually dangerous when disappointment turns into accusation.
“God must not love me.”
“Something must be wrong with me.”
“Maybe I'm being punished.”
“Maybe everyone else is more worthy.”
No.
Your relationship status cannot tell you whether God loves you.
Look somewhere else.
Look at the cross.
If you want to know how seriously God takes sin, look at the cross.
If you want to know how costly grace is, look at the cross.
If you want to know whether Jesus is willing to pursue the undeserving, look at the cross.
And if you want to know whether suffering means God has abandoned His children...
look at the cross again.
The beloved Son suffered.
Pain is not automatic evidence of divine rejection.
Waiting is not automatic evidence of divine neglect.
And marriage is not automatic evidence of divine approval.
Some married people are desperately lonely.
Some single people are profoundly fruitful.
Some marriages beautifully display Christ and His church.
Some singleness beautifully displays that Christ Himself is enough to build a meaningful life around.
Neither relationship status saves anybody.
Jesus does.
Perhaps the hardest possibility to surrender is this:
You may marry someday.
You may not.
Scripture gives us permission to desire marriage.
It gives us wisdom for marriage.
It celebrates marriage.
But it does not authorize us to turn a desire into a prophecy.
There is enormous freedom in refusing to make God sign promises He never wrote.
You don't need another viral Christian post guaranteeing, “Your spouse is closer than you think.”
Maybe they are.
Maybe they aren't.
We don't know.
What we do know is better.
Christ is yours now.
Not someday.
Not after the wedding.
Not when somebody finally recognizes your worth.
Now.
Your life is happening now.
Your calling is happening now.
Your sanctification is happening now.
There are people you can love now.
There are wounds Christ can heal now.
There is Scripture to know now.
There are lonely people you can notice now.
There are unbelievers who need the Gospel now.
There are younger believers who need somebody steady enough to disciple them now.
There are prayers nobody else will pray exactly like you can.
There are acts of generosity you can perform.
There are places you can serve.
There are sins to put to death.
There is holiness to pursue.
There is joy to receive.
There is a Savior to know.
Now.
Do not spend the entire life God has actually given you grieving the imaginary life you thought He was required to give you.
Grieve honestly.
Absolutely.
But don't disappear into the grief.
Bring it to Jesus.
Tell Him when you're lonely.
Tell Him when seeing another engagement hurts.
Tell Him when you're jealous.
Tell Him when you're tired of being the third wheel.
Tell Him when sexual temptation feels unbearable.
Tell Him when you wonder whether anybody will ever know you deeply.
Tell Him the ugly parts too.
He already knows.
Repent where longing has become idolatry.
Receive grace where shame has become your identity.
Ask for wisdom.
Ask for community.
Ask for courage.
Ask for contentment—not the fake contentment that says, “I don't want marriage anymore,” when you still do.
Ask for Christian contentment.
The kind that says:
“Jesus, I still want this. But I want You more. And if I cannot have both today, I will not call You cruel because You have not given me everything I desire.”
That prayer costs something.
But there is freedom on the other side of it.
Paul says in 1 Corinthians 7:35 that he is speaking for the believer's benefit, not to throw a βρόχον—brochon, a restraint or snare—over them.
That detail is beautiful.
Biblical teaching about singleness is not supposed to become another rope around your neck.
Paul isn't trying to imprison single Christians.
He's trying to free their attention for Jesus.
So if church culture has made you feel defective because you're unmarried, Scripture gives you permission to reject that verdict.
If somebody told you that greater faith would guarantee a spouse, reject that promise too.
If somebody made you feel that wanting marriage means Jesus isn't enough, reject that false choice.
You can ache and worship.
You can hope and surrender.
You can desire marriage and refuse to idolize it.
You can ask God boldly and still trust Him when the answer has not arrived.
And you can build a life so deeply rooted in Christ that whether marriage comes next year, ten years from now, or never, Jesus will not have been merely the Person you used to survive the waiting.
He will have been the Treasure.
Maybe that's what someone reading this needs tonight.
Not another prediction.
Not another “God told me your spouse is coming.”
Not another shallow promise designed to make lonely Christians click.
Maybe you need permission to cry...
and then permission to live.
Your singleness is not proof God forgot your address.
He knows where you are.
But the greater miracle of Christianity is not that God knows your street.
It is that through Christ, God knows your name.
And maybe you know someone who has been quietly hurting under the weight of unwanted singleness.
Send this to them.
Not as a hint.
Not as correction.
As companionship.
Someone younger in the faith may need evidence that a meaningful Christian life does not begin at the altar.
Because loneliness has a strange way of making us forget truths we were certain about yesterday.
The Gospel cannot be bought. Grace cannot be purchased.
But supporting faithful Christian work can be one practical way of helping biblical encouragement reach more people.
Then invite someone with you.
A family member.
A struggling believer.
A seeker.
The friend drifting from church.
The Christian whose faith has grown cold.
Even the unbelieving friend who keeps asking difficult questions.
Because maybe the greatest testimony of your single years will not eventually be...
“Then God finally sent me somebody.”
Maybe it will be...
“Jesus became so precious to me that I finally stopped treating the life He had already given me as the hallway to the life I actually wanted.”
And if marriage eventually comes, receive it gratefully.
Love that person sacrificially.
Build something holy together.
But never ask another human being to become what only Christ can be.
And if marriage has not come...
you have not been forgotten.
You have not been demoted.
You have not been sentenced to a meaningless life.
Your story is not waiting for romance before Jesus can write something beautiful with it.
Sometimes the miracle isn't that God finally sends someone. Sometimes the miracle is discovering that while you were staring at the empty chair beside you, Jesus had never left His place beside you.
